author: Athanasius of Alexandria
occasion: Adelphius has written against Arians who refuse to worship the Word with his flesh; Athanasius writes to support his correction and to refute the Arian objection that worshiping Christ in the body means worshiping a creature.
argument: Athanasius praises Adelphius for exposing the Arians' new blasphemy and identifies it with the errors of Valentinus, Marcion, and Mani. He argues that Christians do not worship a creature but the Creator, the Word of God, who became flesh; the flesh is God's own body and temple, and is not to be separated from the Word in worship. The incarnation was for human salvation, deification, and liberation from sin and death, so those who reject or divide the flesh from the Word reject redemption itself. Scripture and apostolic tradition show that the Word acted and suffered in the flesh, and the old temple prefigures the worship due to the Lord in his body. Since the Word is Creator, not creature, his taking a created body does not make him a creature, and the Church worships him as Lord and Creator in the flesh.

outline.move: Athanasius thanks Adelphius, condemns the Arians' new denial of the incarnate presence, and says their error imitates Valentinus, Marcion, and Mani.

He insists Christians worship the Creator Word made flesh, not a creature, and shows from the leper, the woman with the hemorrhage, the sea, the blind man, and the crucifixion that creation recognized its Creator in the body.
He explains that the Son's birth from a woman and the Virgin was for human deification and redemption, and that those who reject or divide the flesh from the Word reject salvation itself.
He cites Peter and Paul to show the Word suffered and gave himself in the flesh, and argues from Israel's worship at the temple that the Lord's body, as the true temple, is worthy of worship.
He concludes that dishonoring the temple dishonors the Lord in it, that a creature cannot save creatures, and that the Church worships the Creator Word who became man for the world's salvation.

cast.name: Athanasius
cast.who: Archbishop of Alexandria and author of the letter.

cast.name: Adelphius
cast.who: Bishop and confessor to whom the letter is addressed.

cast.name: Valentinus
cast.who: Heretic whose teaching made Christ's body a mere appearance.

cast.name: Marcion
cast.who: Heretic associated with those who divided what cannot be divided and denied that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

cast.name: Mani
cast.who: Heretic associated with the same denial of the incarnation.

cast.name: Peter
cast.who: Apostle cited for the divine nature and Christ's suffering in the flesh.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: Apostle cited for Christ's self-giving in the flesh.

cast.name: Stephen
cast.who: The blessed martyr who saw the Lord standing at God's right hand.

cast.name: Gabriel
cast.who: Archangel who announced the Lord's body.

cast.name: Lazarus
cast.who: Raised from the dead by the Word's human voice.

cast.name: Hieracas
cast.who: Presbyter to whom the letter may be read if needed.

voices.speaker: Arians (quoted opponents)
voices.how_marked: Introduced as their invented words or voices, e.g. 'they shout to God saying' and 'they dare to say'; their position is also paraphrased or addressed throughout the letter.

voices.speaker: The Jews
voices.how_marked: Referenced as a comparison group, not given a direct voice; Athanasius asks who would be so impious as to say with the foolish Jews to him: 'Why do you, being a man, make yourself God?'

voices.speaker: The angels
voices.how_marked: Quoted directly with 'said to the disciples'.

voices.speaker: The Lord
voices.how_marked: Quoted directly as speaking to the Father.

voices.speaker: The prophets
voices.how_marked: Quoted directly with 'saying'; the first quotation is from Psalm 42:3 (LXX), the second from Isaiah, so 'prophets' here includes psalmic/prophetic literature broadly.

voices.speaker: Peter
voices.how_marked: Quoted directly with 'saying' in section 4; also cited in section 3 with 'as the blessed Peter wrote'.

voices.speaker: Paul
voices.how_marked: Quoted directly with 'writing' in section 4; also alluded to in section 3 through a Pauline quotation introduced alongside Peter.

key_terms.sense: The Word of God, the Son, Creator of all things, who became flesh.
The flesh or body the Word took in the incarnation, especially as the object of worship and instrument of salvation.
A creature or created thing, contrasted with the Creator; the Arians wrongly call the Word a creature.
The Creator, a title for the Word as maker of all things.
Temple; used both for the old Jerusalem temple and for the Lord's body as the true temple in which God is worshiped.
To worship or bow down before; the central disputed act, whether the Word in the flesh may be worshiped.
The incarnate presence or coming of the Savior in the flesh.
The becoming human of the Word, the incarnation.
To make divine, the purpose of the incarnation for humanity.
Redemption or ransom from sin and death accomplished by Christ in the flesh.
The heretical group Athanasius opposes, who deny the Word's divinity and reject worship of the incarnate Lord.
Mere appearance or illusion, the error of Valentinus and others about Christ's body.

scripture: Athanasius quotes the Septuagint and New Testament. He cites Isaiah, the Psalms, and the Gospels, and refers to Peter and Paul. Psalm numbering follows the Septuagint. Modern citations should use standard English Bible names and, where applicable, note the Septuagint Psalm numbering.
uncertain: The exact date of the letter is not stated in the text; c. 371 is a common scholarly estimate.
The precise identity of Adelphius beyond being a bishop and confessor is not given in the text.
The exact wording of some scriptural quotations may reflect Athanasius's memory or a particular textual tradition.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Marcion: 'Heretic associated with those who divided what cannot be divided and denied that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: οἱ δὲ διαιροῦντες τὰ ἀδιαίρετα ἠρνήσαντο τὸ, Ὁ Λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο, καὶ ἐσκήνωσεν ἐν ἡμῖν
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source groups Valentinus, Marcion, and Mani together as 'those who introduced appearance instead of truth' and 'those who divided what cannot be divided and denied that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.' The brief's phrasing suggests Marcion is specifically associated with the second group, but Athanasius uses plural relative clauses (ὧν οἱ μὲν... οἱ δὲ...) that may distribute differently or apply collectively. More accurate: 'Heretic named alongside Valentinus and Mani; the group collectively introduced appearance instead of truth and/or divided what cannot be divided, denying that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.'

_unresolved_facts.claim: The Jews: 'Referenced as a comparison group, not given a direct voice; Athanasius asks who would be so impious as to say with the foolish Jews to him: "Why do you, being a man, make yourself God?"'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἢ τίς οὕτως ἀσεβής ἐστιν, ὡς μετὰ τῶν ἀφρόνων Ἰουδαίων διὰ τὸ σῶμα λέγειν αὐτῷ· Διὰ τί σὺ, ἄνθρωπος ὢν, ποιεῖς σεαυτὸν Θεόν;
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Jews are given a direct voice: Athanasius asks who would be so impious as to say with the foolish Jews 'through the body' (διὰ τὸ σῶμα) to him: 'Why do you, being a man, make yourself God?' The quotation marks a direct voice attributed to them.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The prophets: 'Quoted directly with "saying"; the first quotation is from Psalm 42:3 (LXX), the second from Isaiah, so "prophets" here includes psalmic/prophetic literature broadly.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: βεβαιουμένη ἔκ τε Νέας καὶ Παλαιᾶς Διαθήκης, τῶν μὲν προφητῶν λεγόντων· Ἀπόστειλον τὸν Λόγον σου καὶ τὴν ἀλήθειάν σου· καὶ, Ἰδοὺ ἡ Παρθένος ἐν γαστρὶ ἕξει καὶ τέξεται Υἱόν, καὶ καλέσουσι τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Ἐμμανουὴλ, ὅ ἐστι μεθερμηνευόμενον, Μεθ' ἡμῶν ὁ Θεός
_unresolved_facts.fix: The first quotation 'Ἀπόστειλον τὸν Λόγον σου καὶ τὴν ἀλήθειάν σου' is from Psalm 42:3 (LXX) / Psalm 43:3 (Hebrew), not from the prophets proper. However, Athanasius explicitly labels both speakers as 'τῶν μὲν προφητῶν' (the prophets). The brief incorrectly states the first is from Psalm 42:3 and the second from Isaiah, then rationalizes 'prophets' broadly. Actually both are introduced as 'prophets saying,' and Athanasius classifies the psalmist as prophet here. The brief's parenthetical about 'psalmic/prophetic literature broadly' is unnecessary speculation—Athanasius simply calls them prophets.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Peter: 'Quoted directly with "saying" in section 4; also cited in section 3 with "as the blessed Peter wrote".'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὡς ἔγραψεν ὁ μακάριος Πέτρος· Καὶ τὸ ἀδύνατον δὲ τοῦ νόμου, ἐν ᾧ ἠσθένει διὰ τῆς σαρκὸς, ὁ Θεὸς τὸν ἑαυτοῦ Υἱὸν πέμψας ἐν ὁμοιώματι σαρκὸς ἁμαρτίας, καὶ περὶ ἁμαρτίας κατέκρινε τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ἐν τῇ σαρκί
_unresolved_facts.fix: In section 3, Peter is cited with 'as the blessed Peter wrote' (ὡς ἔγραψεν ὁ μακάριος Πέτρος), but the quotation that follows ('Καὶ τὸ ἀδύνατον δὲ τοῦ νόμου...') is actually from Romans 8:3, a Pauline text, not from Peter. This is a composite or mistaken attribution in the source. The brief incorrectly states Peter is cited in section 3 without noting this is actually Paul's words. In section 4, Peter is quoted with 'saying' (λέγοντος) for 'Χριστοῦ οὖν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν παθόντος σαρκί' (1 Peter 4:1).

_unresolved_facts.claim: Paul: 'Quoted directly with "writing" in section 4; also alluded to in section 3 through a Pauline quotation introduced alongside Peter.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὡς ἔγραψεν ὁ μακάριος Πέτρος· Καὶ τὸ ἀδύνατον δὲ τοῦ νόμου...
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Pauline quotation in section 3 is explicitly introduced as written by Peter ('ὡς ἔγραψεν ὁ μακάριος Πέτρος'), not 'alongside Peter' or as a Pauline quotation. The brief's 'alluded to in section 3 through a Pauline quotation introduced alongside Peter' misrepresents the attribution. Athanasius attributes Romans 8:3 to Peter here (or the text is composite). The brief should note this is presented as Peter's writing, whether or not modern scholars identify it as Pauline.
